sentences.text: The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — is an adult individual that preserves dorsal vertebrae, ribs, osteoderms, an incomplete foot, and unpublished bones such as a tibia and femur.
Its gently curved dorsal ribs indicate a broad back similar to other ankylosaurs.
The fossil also preserves ossified tendons, a feature also found in ankylosaurs, ornithopods, and possibly Scelidosaurus.

The genus name Dracopelta combines the Latin word for dragon and the Greek word for small shield, while the species name zbyszewskii honors Georges Zbyszewski for his research on Portuguese fossil vertebrates.
Dracopelta is the first recognized ankylosaurid from the Late Jurassic and one of the oldest genera referred to Ankylosauria.
A partial skeleton of Dracopelta was discovered in 1963 or early 1964 during road construction between Barril and Praia da Assenta.
Georges Zbyszewski and Octávio da Veiga Ferreir organized the excavation of the Dracopelta specimen in December 1964.
A nearly complete ankylosaur specimen with a skull, vertebrae, ribs, and a pelvic shield was reported in 2019 from the Lourinhã Formation.
Despite partial remains, Dracopelta is estimated to be around 2 meters long and was likely a quadrupedal herbivore.
Researchers suggest Dracopelta may have had cursorial adaptations based on its autopodial structure resembling that of Scutellosaurus and Scelidosaurus.
Gregory S. Paul estimated Dracopelta to be 3 meters long and weigh 300 kilograms in 2010, while a later publication suggested Dracopelta could have been between 4 and 6 meters long.
Galton originally classified Dracopelta in Nodosauridae in 1980 based on osteoderm morphology.
Vickaryous et al. considered Dracopelta as Ankylosauria incertae sedis, while Carpenter classified it as a nomen dubium within Polacanthidae incertae sedis.
Suberbiola et al. considered Dracopelta a valid taxon based on unique phalangeal and osteoderm morphology.
Dracopelta may share close affinities with Gargoyleosaurus or Mymoorapelta due to faunal similarities.
Dracopelta lived during the Late Jurassic (152.1-145.0 Ma) in the Lourinhã Formation of Portugal.
The holotype was found in the Assenta Member of the Lourinhã Formation dating to the uppermost lower and upper Tithonian stages.
The Assenta Member represents a fluvial environment with preserved coalified plant fragments.
Dracopelta coexisted with Lusovenator, turiasaurian sauropods, crocodylomorphs, and another indeterminate ankylosaur.
